prompt: A fixed-window limiter grants a full quota in each calendar minute. A client uses its quota just before the minute changes, then sends another burst just after. What weakness does this expose?

options.text: Both windows can admit their quota, causing a large short burst across the boundary.
options.explanation: Correct. Separate window counts do not enforce the same quota over every rolling interval.

options.text: The new minute must inherit the previous minute’s full count.
options.explanation: That would be a different algorithm; this one resets at the boundary.

options.text: The limiter queues the second burst and releases it smoothly.
options.explanation: A fixed-window counter does not imply a queue or pacing.

options.text: The behaviour occurs only if the counter update races.
options.explanation: Even a perfectly atomic fixed-window counter has this boundary property.

workedExample: The limiter sees two different accounting windows. Each burst can be valid within its own window even though they arrive almost together. Use a rolling count when that is the requirement, or a queue with controlled release when downstream pacing is the objective.

link.title: Cloudflare blog: Counting things, a lot of different things

prompt: A legacy mainframe behind your API can handle at most 50 requests/s and falls over with bursts. Clients send bursty traffic averaging 40 req/s. Which algorithm best protects the mainframe?

options.explanation: A large-capacity token bucket deliberately *allows* bursts of up to 500 requests at once, which is exactly what the mainframe can't handle.
Correct. A leaky bucket queues incoming bursts and releases them at a constant rate, so the mainframe never sees more than 50 req/s. The trade-off is added latency while requests wait in the queue.
3,000/min averages 50/s, but a fixed window lets all 3,000 through in the first second of the minute, which would flatten the mainframe.

options.text: No limiter, because the average is below 50 req/s
options.explanation: The average is fine; the *bursts* are the problem. Without shaping, a spike of 200 in one second will exceed capacity.

workedExample: The mainframe needs paced arrivals, not merely a low average. A bounded queue draining at a controlled rate smooths admitted bursts. Reject excess work when the queue is full and bound queueing delay; otherwise protecting throughput could create unacceptable latency. A large token bucket or minute counter still permits damaging short bursts.
